summary: Defines an HTTP response header field called Safe, which a server can use to say that repeating a request is safe. This would let browsers retry some requests, such as certain POSTs, without bothering the user. The document is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A little label a website can attach to say it is fine to press the button again. Browsers could then retry without asking you.

questions: what is the http safe header
is it safe to retry an http post
when does a browser need to ask permission to retry
what does a safe request mean
subtitle: Telling browsers when it is safe to retry an HTTP request.

tldr.problem: Browsers need explicit user confirmation to retry unsafe requests like POST, creating confusing dialogs that slow navigation. Sometimes a POST request is actually safe to repeat without side effects.
tldr.mechanism: The Safe header field lets servers indicate whether repeating a received request is safe, so browsers can retry without asking the user.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now Historic and was never widely adopted, as modern HTTP semantics handle this better with methods like PUT and PATCH.

today: RFC 2310 is now marked Historic and was never widely adopted. Modern HTTP uses semantically appropriate methods like PUT and PATCH instead of relying on a Safe header to indicate POST safety.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2310 defines the Safe HTTP response header field, which origin servers use to indicate whether repeating an HTTP request is safe. A request is safe when it does not cause side effects for which the user will be held accountable.

Repeating a POST request requires explicit user confirmation in HTTP/1.1 by default, but when the POST is actually safe, servers can signal this with the Safe header to let browsers retry automatically without the confusing confirmation dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The Safe header tells a browser: this request will not cause trouble if you do it again, so you do not need to ask the user.

sections.title: When Retries Happen
sections.content:
User agents need to repeat requests in several situations: when a network error leaves the result indeterminate, when the user presses reload while viewing a response, or when the browser history function redisplays a past response. In these cases, if the original POST request is unsafe, HTTP requires explicit user confirmation before repeating it.

If the POST is safe, the confirmation dialog can be omitted entirely. Web applications that need POST for large form data, file uploads, or security reasons can benefit from signaling safety to the browser.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you need to ask the browser to send the same request again—maybe the network broke, or you clicked back. If the server says it is safe, the browser just does it instead of bugging you.

sections.title: The Safe Header
sections.content:
The Safe response header field uses simple syntax: the field name followed by either yes or no. For example, a server sends Safe: yes to indicate the request is safe to repeat.

A request is considered a repetition of a previous request if issued by the same user agent, applied to the same resource, using the same method, and with identical request bodies (after decoding). If the Safe header is absent, the request is assumed unsafe unless it is GET or HEAD, which are safe by definition.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is just a tiny label: Safe: yes or Safe: no. It tells the browser which requests are really safe to try again.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC notes that the Safe header introduces no new security risks beyond those of HTTP form submission. The specification refers to RFC 2068 (HTTP/1.1) for a full discussion of security considerations with HTTP form submission. Using GET requests for form submission has security risks absent in POST submission, and the Safe header may improve overall security by reducing incentives to misuse GET for forms.
sections.plainLanguage: The Safe header itself does not create new dangers. It actually helps because it makes it safer to use POST instead of GET for sending form data.
